newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-VON GRUENIGEN SHYS AWAY FROM THE SPOTLIGHT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-VON GRUENIGEN SHYS AWAY FROM THE SPOTLIGHT.

text.p: Switzerland's Michael Von Gruenigen and Alpine skiing rival Alberto Tomba offer a study in contrasts.
Von Gruenigen avoids the spotlight with the same passion the Italian seeks it out.
After winning the first gold medal of his career in Wednesday's world championship giant slalom to dethrone local hero Tomba, Von Gruenigen remained a picture of composure.

"I am a calm type of person. I cannot pretend to be something I am not, not even for the sport," said the 27-year-old Swiss, who did little more than raise his arms in delight after crossing the finish line.
Tomba's response to success is quite different.
The 30-year-old bachelor, who lives with his wealthy parents outside Bologna, rolls around in the snow, hugs his coaches and visibly enjoys the media fuss surrounding him.
Von Gruenigen shys away from media attention. "I don't read any newspapers over the winter. My wife saves them all for me. I look at them at the end of the season," he said.
Unlike the flamboyant Italian, Von Gruenigen was brought up by his older sister Christine -- a former skier on the Swiss team -- following the death of his parents.

The most important thing in the life of MVG -- as he is nicknamed in his ski-crazed country -- is his wife and two-year-old son and he said he spent the interval between championship runs together with them.
Tomba headed for lunch after crashing out of the first run, but not before pleasing his many fans by signing autographs.

Von Gruenigen, the runaway leader in the giant slalom World Cup standings and winner of two giant slaloms, said Tomba's decision to miss most of the winter's races to give the championships priority was unfair on other racers.
"If Tomba chooses to concentrate only on the championships then that is his decision. But it is not fair on all the other skiers who take part in the long World Cup season.
"I consider the World Cup more important than championships, which are a one-day event. So much can go wrong on that one day, you need a lot of luck," he said.
Tomba missed the first few races after sustaining a wrist and knee injury in a heavy fall during training before the start of the season and was sidelined by influenza earlier in January.
He has repeatedly criticised the World Cup format, threatening to skip races when it suits him.
The Italian won the slalom in Schladming two weeks ago and finished second twice, but failed to complete the only giant slalom he participated in at Kranjska Gora.
"It was his (Tomba) decision not to compete in all giant slaloms. But he has to realize his competitors are not sleeping. I never saw him as a threat," said Von Gruenigen.
"Our giant slalom technique is constantly changing. If he doesn't keep up and learn it, then it is his own problem."
But despite his cool manner, Von Gruenigen admitted to being delighted with his medal.
"Of course I am happy with this title. It is something every skier dreams about his whole career," he said. "But it is not easy to programme yourself to be 100 percent on a particular day."
